articles.title: New blood test claims to detect 50-plus cancers before symptoms – but there’s no evidence it can reduce your risk of dying from cancer
articles.author: Andrew Wolf, Professor Emeritus of Medicine, University of Virginia
paras: Cancer isn’t the leading cause of death in the United States; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it’s cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans.

Cancer can take an excruciating toll on its millions of victims and their family members. Cancer treatments are often highly toxic, and the disease is increasingly striking people at younger ages, which is why it accounts for more years of potential life lost than heart disease.

So when a blood test comes along that claims to be able to screen for over 50 cancers at once in a single blood draw before symptoms appear – as is the case for the Galleri test, by the biotech company GRAIL – it might seem like society has a Holy Grail of modern medicine at their fingertips.
But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the Galleri test is not yet the universal screening breakthrough patients and doctors hope for.
As a physician who studies early cancer detection, and as chair of the American Cancer Society’s screening guideline development group, I have been following this test’s development with interest.

While the Galleri test certainly shows great promise, clinical trial data indicates that it struggles with early-stage cancer detection and has not yet been shown to lower the risk of death from cancer or prevent advanced cancer. Across all cancer stages, the test missed over two-thirds of cancer cases.

On Sept. 23, 2026, an advisory panel to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration voted to recommend approval of the Galleri test. While a recommendation from the FDA’s advisory panel is not the same as full approval from the agency, it marks a critical first step in the process of potentially making the test widely available to the American public. The FDA has not yet announced when it will make a decision on the test.

But even as the advisory panel approved the test, panelists recommended that the word “early” be removed from “early cancer detection test” in product labeling. Panel members were not convinced the test can find cancers at their earliest and most curable stages, and they expressed uncertainty about the test’s benefit to patients at this time.
Given this uncertainty, careful scrutiny of the data behind the test can help doctors and patients make informed decisions about whether to use it.
What is the Galleri test? How does it work?

Galleri is part of an emerging class of multicancer early detection tests. These tests do not diagnose cancer: If a test is positive, further evaluation is necessary to determine whether cancer is present, and, if so, what type of cancer. It is offered as a screening test, similar to mammography for breast cancer screening or PSA testing for prostate cancer screening, but with the potential advantage of screening for many cancers at once, including many for which no screening test currently exists.

The Galleri test looks for DNA fragments in blood that are associated with cancer. When something goes wrong with your DNA, whether because you inherited a mutation or something in your environment triggered that mutation, the processes that regulate cell division can go awry. Uncontrolled cell division can trigger the growth of cancer cells.

Galleri and other multicancer early detection tests in development look for differences that distinguish the DNA produced by tumor cells from normal cells. Galleri identifies unique tags on cancer DNA called methylation markers and uses machine learning algorithms to generate a positive or negative test result.
What are the strengths of the Galleri test?

The Galleri test looks for DNA signals from over 50 cancers, including the 12 that account for almost two-thirds of cancer deaths in the U.S, such as lung and pancreas cancer. Importantly, it provides information on which organ the possible tumor likely originated from. Currently recommended cancer screenings are largely limited to four types of cancer.

Many of the cancers the Galleri test looks for are not currently included in routine screening. Moreover, the test has a very low false positive rate: Only about 0.5% of people who get the test are incorrectly identified as having cancer, or one person out of every 200 tests. A false positive rate is the percentage of people who are told they have cancer but actually don’t. This requires that patients get more testing, which can be costly, sometimes risky and often worrisome.
In comparison, many currently recommended screening tests, such as the Cologuard stool test for colorectal cancer, have false positive rates in the 10% range.

This very low false positive rate also translates into another strength – a very high positive predictive value, or PPV, which is the probability that a positive test result actually means cancer is present. The PPV of the Galleri test was 52% across three annual screens, meaning over half the positive results actually led to a cancer diagnosis. This is good because it gives people confidence that the test is more than 50% correct.

For context, the PPVs of most recommended screening tests – such as stool tests for colorectal cancer, mammography for breast cancer, or the HPV test for cervical cancer – are typically below 10%, meaning most positive results don’t lead to a cancer diagnosis.

The Galleri test also can predict with high accuracy where a cancer originated in the body. In one study of 32,000 U.S. adults age 50 and older who received a Galleri blood test, cancer was diagnosed in about 0.5% of them – 173 patients. Of these patients, the test correctly predicted the cancer type in 91%. This specificity could help clinicians select more targeted evaluations rather than looking for cancer anywhere in the body.
What are the limitations of the Galleri test?
Despite these impressive results, the Galleri test has several major shortcomings.

For one, the test is not as good at detecting cancer in its earliest stages as currently recommended screening tests, which is the main point of a cancer screening test. The test’s ability to detect cancer at all stages was less than 31% over three annual rounds of screening, meaning the test missed 69% of cases. Of the cancers detected in the study, comparing outcomes from getting the Galleri test three years in a row to routine cancer screening, 60% of the cancers detected in the people who got the Galleri test were early stage, which was almost identical to those who didn’t get it.

In addition, the Galleri test did not perform any better than standard screening tests at detecting cancer early. The detection rate for early-stage cancers was only 21% over three years of screening, meaning almost 80% were missed. Cancer is most curable in its early stages, so this shortcoming is a major one. Such a low detection rate can lead to false reassurance from an incorrectly negative test result.

Perhaps the most important shortcoming of the Galleri test is that it hasn’t yet proved that it can save lives or even reduce the risk of being diagnosed with late-stage cancer. The main goal of the trial was to show that the test could reduce the incidence of late-stage cancers over three years of screening – and it failed to do so. In other words, one of the hopes was that the test could reduce the risk of being diagnosed with advanced cancer by finding and treating cancer early – but as of now, there is no evidence to support this.

There was a hint that the incidence of Stage 4 cancer was trending lower by the third year of screening. But more time is needed to determine whether this is a true finding and, if so, whether it leads to a lower risk of dying from cancer.
Requests for comment from GRAIL were not returned.
What did the FDA’s panel recommend?
The FDA advisory panel took three votes. While one of of these votes followed the evidence, two of them were surprisingly counterintuitive.

First, the panel voted 10-0 to recommend that the Galleri test is safe. While undergoing a blood test doesn’t typically involve any substantive risk, a positive result may prompt further testing, such as biopsies, that are riskier than a blood test and can incur additional costs.

These harms can be particularly hard to swallow if the test turns out to be a false alarm, as it will in about half of cases. One study evaluating Galleri’s safety found that 0.6% of those who had the test ended up undergoing an invasive diagnostic procedure, but none experienced serious complications. Hence, the safety vote appears to have been warranted.

Second, the panel voted 6-4 to recommend that the test is effective, though a number of the panelists cast their yes vote on the condition that the company remove the term “early” from the label “multi-cancer early detection” test.

This outcome, however, does not have the evidence to back it up. Available studies indicate the Galleri test does not reduce the incidence of late-stage cancer and performs poorly in detecting early-stage cancer. Additionally, there is no evidence that it lowers the risk of dying from cancer.

Finally, the panel voted 7-2 with one abstention to recommend that the benefits of the Galleri test outweigh the risk. But if there is no proven benefit to the test, how can the benefits outweigh the risks, even if the risk is low?

While the advisory panel acknowledged the test’s serious limitations, it still went ahead and recommended approval. One of the panel members stated that the ability to find more early-stage cancers in a broader population is a benefit, even though that hasn’t been proved yet. “So perhaps my ‘yes’ is a hopeful (vote) rather than an accurate one,” said the panel member.
The problem is that “hope” does not reduce death and disability from cancer.
Should you get the Galleri test or not?

If the FDA agrees with its advisory panel’s recommendation and approves the Galleri test, it will likely be more widely marketed to the American public. Regardless, there remain many caveats, and I believe patients will want to be cautious.

First, FDA approval does not guarantee insurance coverage. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has a separate coverage determination process, and it is not required to grant coverage to FDA-approved tests. The out-of-pocket cost of the Galleri test is currently US$949.

It remains unclear whether the test can reduce your risk of dying from cancer or being diagnosed with advanced cancer. However, if you’re willing to pay the annual cost of the test, are willing to undergo further testing despite a high rate of false alarms, and are not overly reassured by a falsely negative test result, you can ask your doctor for more information about the test.

What doctors and researchers are certain about is the importance of staying up to date with currently recommended cancer screening tests for colon, breast, cervical and lung cancers, even if you decide to get the Galleri test. These tests are proven to detect early-stage cancer and lower your risk of dying from cancer. That’s the bottom line.

Andrew Wolf serves as Chair of the American Cancer Society's Guideline Development Group. This is a volunteer position. Opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the American Cancer Society.

articles.title: Why do farts smell so bad? A microbiologist explains the odors brewing in your gut
articles.author: Brenda A. Wilson, Professor of Microbiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why do farts smell so bad? – Daisy, age 7, New York, New York
A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. All together, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an important job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

As a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.
So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?
Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

Anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

But wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

One key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

Only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.
Your gut’s source of grody gases
The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.
However, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

When you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

As you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

Farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness book of world records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mis-hears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

But sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves and volcano vents that can suffocate and kill you.
So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

articles.title: For veterans with mild traumatic brain injury, a restaurant or other noisy environment can feel like a battlefield
articles.author: Jeffrey Hebert, Associate Professor of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, University of Colorado Anschutz
paras: Imagine sitting down with your family at a restaurant. Conversations at your table overlap with those of patrons seated nearby. Utensils clink on plates. Waitstaff weave between tables. Music plays overhead.

Many people might find the bustle of such a scene a bit annoying. However, for veterans with chronic mild traumatic brain injury, or TBI, also referred to as concussion, busy environments like this are frequently intolerable. What should be an enjoyable social event soon escalates to internal mayhem. They find their attention stretched beyond capacity. Tension and irritability grow. The impulse to flee or fight becomes paramount.
Veterans who have chronic mild TBI and have described these experiences to me often ask: “Why does this keep happening?”

I am a clinical neuroscientist providing treatment and rehabilitation at an institute in Colorado for military service members and veterans who have experienced concussions. Some of the most common challenges I see in my patients are irritability and cognitive problems. With this knowledge, my scientific efforts focus on discovering the causes of these persistent symptoms.

My colleagues’ and my research is revealing that these challenges may largely be due to the injured brain being flooded by sensory information that overwhelms its processing capacity. This may explain why even a mild brain injury can interfere with military service members’ transition to civilian life.

Mild TBIs are among the most common injuries that military service members experience and are considered the signature injury of recent wars and ongoing conflicts. Since 2000, more than 500,000 military service members have experienced a TBI, according to the Defense Health Agency. More than four out of five of these injuries are classified as “mild”.

Many people appear to recover quickly from these injuries, within weeks or a couple of months, but for a considerable number of others, symptoms and measurable brain changes persist years or even decades later.

Military service members and veterans often experience post-traumatic stress and mild TBI together. Studies have linked the two conditions collectively to changes in behavior, cognitive complaints and negative impact on their spousal relationship and family satisfaction and functioning.

Addressing these issues solely through a psychological lens has its limits, since many of these problems happen while the veteran is trying to function in environments that can lead to sensory overload.
A sensory bottleneck in the injured brain

Throughout the day, the human brain is tasked with managing multiple sensory inputs. It is constantly working to pay attention to what’s most relevant while filtering out whatever might distract it from functioning properly.
But for the injured brain, the filtering process often malfunctions. This can create a bottleneck of sensory information, which stresses the brain’s processing capacity.

In a 2026 study of military veterans, my colleagues and I found that in people with chronic mild TBI, symptoms of irritability were intertwined with post-traumatic stress symptoms and sensory problems such as pain and difficulties processing speech in noisy environments.

In other words, veterans with chronic mild TBI are simultaneously trying to manage ongoing pain, distinguish speech from competing sounds, maintain attention and regulate emotional responses. That may be why busy environments are so burdensome for them: These demands deplete the brain’s bandwidth, pushing it beyond its threshold.
The consequences of visual challenges

In another recent study, my research team and I found that veterans with chronic mild traumatic brain injury experience difficulties such as quick eye movements and challenges with cognition, including attention, impulsivity and verbal fluency.

Crowded restaurants, grocery stores, airports and family gatherings contain a great deal of visual motion. One of the vision tests in the study is similar to the problem our veterans face in these real-world environments. In these environments, the inability to stop getting distracted by movement in their vision, often referred to as the “squirrel” moment, is a consistent complaint. In our study, we found that the difficulty suppressing that impulse is a problem for veterans with chronic mild TBI and is directly associated with their ongoing difficulties in attention, impulsivity and processing speed.

Increased visual stimulation creates more cognitive load, consuming resources the brain needs to manage other demands. For example, the injured brain also needs to simultaneously manage psychological stress, pain and sound that further deplete the brain’s reserves.
Everyone is equipped with a limited amount of brain and cognitive reserves.

Healthier brains tend to have a larger reserve that withstands onslaughts of sensory stimuli and challenges to emotional and cognitive control. In contrast, the injured brain has a limited reserve or threshold, leading to irritability, poor attention and impulsivity, making socializing with family and friends intolerable.

These limitations aren’t simply an annoyance or added challenge; they test the brain’s ability to continuously, efficiently and effectively process and respond to a world filled with constant incoming sensory data.
For veterans living with the long-term effects of mild TBI, understanding this paradox can often be one of the most important steps toward seeking the most appropriate care.

Jeffrey Hebert receives funding from the Department of Defense, the Avalon Action Alliance Medical Research Award Program, the Marcus Institute for Brain Health. He is affiliated with the International Concussion Society as a Science & Performance Advisory Board Member.

articles.title: Back pain: how your doctor’s words could influence your recovery
articles.author: Dave Newell, Professor of Integrated Musculoskeletal Care and Head of the Centre of Pain and Active Inference Research, Health Sciences University
paras: Jenny’s back pain usually settles within a few weeks. This time, 12 weeks have passed and it still intrudes on her life. Getting dressed hurts. Sitting through work is difficult. And something else is becoming harder to ignore: worry.
Why hasn’t it gone away? Is something seriously wrong? Will it ever get better?
Social media offers plenty of alarming possibilities. Jenny starts monitoring every twinge. Each painful movement seems to confirm that something must be wrong.

Jenny is fictional, but her experience may be familiar. When she consults her doctor, she might expect relief from exercise, medication or hands-on treatment. Could the consultation itself also influence her pain?

Imagine two versions of Jenny’s appointment. In one, the doctor interrupts her and describes her back as “worn out”. Jenny leaves with exercises, but also with a disturbing picture of a fragile spine.

In the other, the doctor listens, explores her concerns and examines her carefully. Finding no signs suggesting a serious underlying cause, they explain what they have assessed, acknowledge how disabling her pain is and discuss a manageable plan.
Both appointments might include the same exercises, but Jenny may leave with different expectations about her back.
Researchers call these surrounding influences “contextual factors”. They include expectations, past experiences, the doctor’s communication and the care setting.

Studies suggest these factors are linked to treatment outcomes. In one study involving 182 people with longstanding back pain, a stronger relationship with their physiotherapist early in treatment was associated with better outcomes after eight weeks.

Another UK study involving 960 patients receiving physiotherapy, osteopathy or acupuncture found that the relationship between patient and practitioner was among the strongest predictors of reduced disability. Agreement about treatment goals and how to achieve them was particularly important.
These observational studies cannot establish that the relationship caused improvement, but they suggest that what happens during a consultation deserves attention.
How words can influence pain
If Jenny’s pain is in her back, how could someone’s manner or explanation influence it?
Pain is not a straightforward measure of damage: its intensity does not always match the extent of tissue injury.

One possible explanation comes from predictive processing theories. These suggest that the nervous system interprets signals from the body alongside previous experiences, expectations and present circumstances.

For Jenny, pain that once meant “another episode that will settle” may now mean “something dangerous that nobody has identified”. This change in expectation could contribute to her pain feeling more threatening.
This is one possible explanation of persistent pain. It does not mean Jenny has consciously caused her symptoms.

There is experimental evidence that expectations can influence pain. In one study, healthy volunteers received a powerful opioid painkiller while experiencing painful heat. Positive expectations roughly doubled the drug’s pain-relieving effect, while negative expectations abolished it.
The drug was still being delivered, but participants received different information about it. Brain scans also showed changes in activity in regions involved in processing pain.

This suggests that expectations can influence pain through measurable biological processes. However, findings from short laboratory experiments cannot tell us exactly how much a particular consultation will affect someone with longstanding back pain.
Giving reassurance something to stand on
Simply saying “there’s nothing wrong” is unlikely to address Jenny’s experience. Something plainly is wrong: she hurts, cannot do what she normally does and wants to understand why.
A useful explanation would acknowledge this while distinguishing pain from evidence of serious disease. It would explain the assessment and give Jenny opportunities to ask questions.
The doctor might also ask what she fears. Perhaps her main worry is that bending will damage her spine. Exercises alone may leave that concern untouched.

A theory called “active inference” offers another way to understand this. It proposes that expectations influence what people do, while their actions provide new information that can change those expectations.

In a 2026 paper applying this approach to pain affecting muscles and joints, researchers suggest that movement, communication and other aspects of care may help patients develop different expectations about their bodies.

If Jenny expects bending to cause damage, she may avoid it. With appropriate clinical guidance, gradually exploring that movement could help her discover that her back is more capable than she feared.

This theory may help explain how care works, but researchers have not shown that applying it improves outcomes beyond existing treatments. Treatments also have specific effects that cannot be explained by context alone.

A reassuring consultation cannot replace appropriate assessment or effective treatment, repair an injury or guarantee recovery. Nor does the importance of context justify offering unproven treatments simply because they are delivered with a good bedside manner.
Patients should never be blamed for continuing pain or told they need to think positively.

For doctor, the practical message is to combine careful assessment and evidence-based treatment with explanations that inform without creating unnecessary alarm. UK clinical guidance supports shared decisions, advice about remaining active and individually appropriate treatment for lower back pain.
Patients can reasonably ask what might be causing their pain, whether there are signs of anything serious and what activities they can safely continue.

Jenny needs her pain taken seriously, her concerns heard and a credible way forward. The way that care is offered may help shape what happens next, including her confidence in moving and managing pain.

articles.title: A brief history of the food pyramid – and its many false starts
articles.author: Anna Stubbendorff, Postdoctoral Fellow, Nutrition Epidemiology, Lund University
paras: The food pyramid has made an unlikely comeback. In January 2026, the US government unveiled an upside-down version, giving prominence to foods such as red meat and full-fat dairy.

More recently, an international team of researchers, led by Brigham Young University in the US, proposed a very different food pyramid built around vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and other plant foods. They call it the International Food Guide Pyramid.

The two designs reflect different views about what a healthy diet should look like. They also revive an old question: how do you turn complex nutritional evidence into a simple picture that helps people decide what to eat?
The history of the food pyramid shows that its design has been shaped by politics, commercial interests as well as scientific advice.

The idea began in Sweden in 1974 when a food educator devised a pyramid to show people how much of different foods they should eat. Rising food prices had prompted an investigation into eating nutritiously on a budget.
The pyramid’s broad base contained affordable everyday foods: bread, cereals, potatoes, milk, cheese and cooking fats. Fruit and vegetables occupied the middle, with meat, fish and eggs at the top.

Before food pyramids, we had food circles, which gave equal space to all food groups. Pyramids added the proportions. Their broad base and narrow peak suggested that people should eat more of some foods than others.

Food pyramids were based on nutrient requirements, food costs and practical teaching. Their aim was to turn nutrition knowledge into shopping and cooking decisions, rather than to offer direct evidence that following the pyramid would prevent disease.

The US arrived at its own pyramid more slowly. In April 1991, the US agriculture department withdrew its planned pyramid after meat and dairy organisations objected to their products’ placement near the top. The department said more consumer testing was needed.
US designers then considered bowls, shopping carts, wheels, fans and picnic scenes. After further testing, the pyramid won out, and the Food Guide Pyramid was published in 1992.

Bread, cereals, rice and pasta filled its base, with six to 11 servings a day recommended. A serving was smaller than many modern portions: one slice of bread or half a cup (around 70g) of cooked pasta. The range reflected different calorie needs, so 11 servings was never the advice for everyone.

The picture failed to distinguish clearly between wholegrains and refined grains. It also grouped oils with fats and sweets at the tip, obscuring differences between healthier plant oils and fats such as butter. Yet the accompanying booklet did recommend wholegrains: some advice disappeared when the image travelled alone.

The 2005 makeover, MyPyramid, replaced horizontal layers with coloured vertical stripes. A figure climbing steps represented the importance of physical activity. Much of the explanation moved online, leaving an image that offered few clues about what to put on a dinner plate.

In 2011, a dinner plate replaced the pyramid in the US. The US Department of Agriculture’s MyPlate showed fruit and vegetables filling half a plate, with grains and protein foods sharing the remainder and dairy alongside. It made the advice easier to relate to a meal.
Sweden had already developed a plate model in the late 1970s, using three sections to show the balance between vegetables, starchy foods and protein sources within a meal.

The Swedish plate was updated in 2016 to reflect different dietary choices, such as beans and tofu in the protein section. It now has three versions for different populations; one for people who meet physical activity recommendations, one for those who are less active and therefore need less energy, and one for older adults with poor appetite.

Canada’s plate, published in 2019, highlights a bigger proportion of vegetables and fruits and a smaller proportion of wholegrain foods and protein foods (also emphasising different sources of protein).

The Mediterranean pyramid, published in 2011, went further by including shared meals, cooking, exercise and rest alongside food. Other countries developed their own food guides, reflecting local diets and traditions.

In January 2026, the US government brought back the food pyramid, this time upside down. Its emphasis on red meat and full-fat dairy has drawn criticism for sending mixed messages about saturated fat, while giving wholegrains less prominence.

Experts have questioned the scientific basis of some recommendations, arguing that the government sidelined its independent advisory committee’s findings and used a less transparent review process. Cardiology specialists have also challenged the promotion of butter and beef fat, pointing to evidence favouring liquid plant oils for heart health.

The more recent International Food Guide Pyramid, published in the journal Advances in Nutrition, combines research and national dietary guidelines. Its proportions draw on the Eat-Lancet reference diet, which sets out how people could eat healthily while reducing the damage food production does to the planet.

Its recommendations emphasise vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, beans, lentils, nuts and plant oils. Animal foods fit in smaller amounts. The pyramid judges carbohydrates by fibre, food structure and effects on blood sugar, rather than simply by quantity.

Fish and poultry are preferred over red and processed meat, and vegetarian and vegan versions of the pattern are possible. The intention is to allow people to use foods available and familiar where they live.
The authors report no funding for this study, although several disclose financial relationships with food companies. It is a proposal, not an official replacement for national dietary guidelines.
Different pictures for different jobs
The food pyramid has been redesigned many times, reflecting changes in nutrition science and in how advice is communicated. Different images do different jobs.
A food circle shows variety across food groups, a pyramid may guide the weekly shop, and a plate helps balance a single meal. Dietitians and teachers can use them together.

The new Advances in Nutrition paper does not test whether people understand or follow its pyramid better than a plate. For someone preparing dinner, the useful question is whether the image makes everyday choices easier: beans more often, wholegrain bread instead of white, or olive oil instead of butter.
Whatever its shape, a food guide has to translate into meals that people can afford and enjoy.

articles.title: Dark nutrition: what happens when people stop trusting food and nutrition science?
articles.author: Jordan Beaumont, Senior Lecturer in Food and Nutrition, Sheffield Hallam University
paras: “I’m Pi and this is Leo, and today we’re going to eat some raw roadkill.” So begins a YouTube video featuring two raw food enthusiasts eating the heart of a run-over raccoon.
Another of the duo’s YouTube videos is titled The Elite Know Raw Food is Safe & Healthy and Vilify it to Keep You a Weak Slave. That title neatly sums up the ethos of “dark nutrition”.

A New York Times Magazine article clarifies that dark nutrition is not a specific diet, but a style of thinking about food and health. “Its adherents [have] concluded that the usual sources of authority – doctors, public health officials, food executives, pharmaceutical corporations – [can] not be trusted,” the article explains.

People who follow this style of eating tend to reject mainstream dietary advice in favour of unconventional eating practices. This can include avoiding seed oils, drinking unpasteurised milk, consuming lots of sugar, avoiding vegetables, taking unusually high doses of supplements and, yes, even eating raw roadkill.

These food choices often stem from concerns about pesticides, toxins and pollutants in food. Or they can emerge when someone has an ailment their doctor can’t resolve. They take matters into their own hands and change the one thing they have complete control over: their diet.

Most people are satisfied with official nutritional guidance, but others seek more specific answers. As a result, those following dark nutrition self-experiment in an attempt to boost their health or treat a condition, regardless of whether there is scientific evidence to support their choices.

Some people get their nutrition information from the news, social media, and family and friends. But what is often covered in the headlines or on social media isn’t necessarily what is shown in the scientific studies.

The misleading information could be because journalists and influencers are not trained to understand the complex content of research papers, or because researchers are just really bad at explaining their findings. Even healthcare professionals and the government get it wrong occasionally. As a result, nutrition messages can become confused and confusing.

A great example is the humble egg. In 1957, the British Egg Marketing Board launched the campaign: “Go to work on an egg”. Then, in 1968, the American Heart Association recommended that people at high risk of heart disease eat no more than three eggs a week.

The recommendation was based partly on animal experiments linking blood cholesterol to coronary heart disease. However, the relationship between eating eggs and developing heart disease turned out to be considerably more complicated than early nutritional advice suggested.
By the 1990s, eggs were back in the good books. They are now widely considered a healthy and affordable source of protein, vitamins and minerals.
Margarine, red wine, coffee, coconut oil, red meat, potatoes and chocolate have had their own roller-coaster rides – one minute healthy, the next minute not.

This constant back-and-forth and changing messages can mean it is hard to know what constitutes a healthy diet. Unfortunately, nutrition science is messy, and it is a relatively young scientific discipline. Much of what we know has only been identified in the last century.
That means there are lots of questions that remain unanswered, and as we (nutritionists) search for the answers, we are likely to get things wrong. That is science.

Science is a process of questioning the world around us and searching for answers through research. The problem we have in nutrition research is that it is very hard to control someone’s diet and all the factors in their life that can affect health to provide definitive answers to the questions.

We mainly rely on people self-reporting the foods they eat and what illnesses or diseases they develop. This can tell us whether there is a link between diet and health, but not if diet prevents or causes illness and disease. So we have evidence that is seen as broad, conflicting and confusing.

Sadly, we now live in a post-truth era where scientific evidence is less important and influential than someone’s beliefs or opinions. The influencer culture – where people can share their own thoughts as fact, regardless of whether there is any foundation or evidence – has a big role to play in fuelling dark nutrition.

What is clear here is that the wider dangers of following dark nutrition are largely ignored. The potential for food poisoning, infection and disease by eating raw meat and organs, the risk of vitamin and mineral deficiencies by avoiding fruit and vegetables, and the chance of toxic levels of some vitamins and minerals with excessive supplement use.

It can be confusing to know what to eat. Government guidelines on food and nutrition remain the backbone of a healthy diet, and these will develop as new evidence emerges. Questioning conventional advice is reasonable, but alternative diets also need to be judged by the quality of the evidence.

Jordan Beaumont receives funding from the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) and Sheffield Children's Hospital Charity Trust. He is affiliated with the Association for the Study of Obesity and the Faculty of Public Health.

articles.title: Sewers could hold the key to detecting deadly fungal infections
articles.author: Pooja Padmakumar, PhD Candidate in Environmental Science, Bangor University
paras: Every year, fungal infections kill around 2.5 million people worldwide, more than tuberculosis and malaria combined. Yet most people may have never heard of the fungi responsible, and few health systems track them in any organised way.
In a recent review, my colleagues and I argue that one of the best places to start looking for these fungal pathogens is the sewer.

Fungi are all around us and most are harmless. A small number cause serious disease, mainly in people whose immune systems are weakened, for example by cancer treatment, an organ transplant or a stay in intensive care. The World Health Organization has published a list of priority fungal pathogens that it says urgently need better surveillance.

A warming climate, more people living with weakened immunity and a very small number of antifungal drugs are creating good conditions for dangerous fungi, so this threat is growing. Some are adapting to human body temperature, to hospital environments and to the medicines used against them.

One example is Candida auris. It was first identified in a patient’s ear in Japan in 2009. This yeast has since spread worldwide, it resists several drugs and it causes hospital outbreaks that are hard to control.

Despite this, fungi get little attention. Unlike flu or norovirus, fungal infections rarely look like an outbreak. They tend to be seen as a complication of someone’s existing illness rather than a public health threat in their own right. In the UK, labs have only been required to report C. auris since 2025.

In our review, we looked at why hospital-based monitoring misses fungi, and at what the early evidence says about testing wastewater instead. We found three main problems. The first is the one above: fungi are treated as a secondary concern.

The second is biology. Many people carry fungi such as Candida on their skin or in their gut for months or even years without feeling ill, and the whole time they are shedding the fungus. Hospital testing only picks up the minority who become seriously ill, so the true spread is underestimated.

The third problem is technical limitations. Fungal tests are limited, and there is little commercial incentive to improve them. Labs often don’t identify common yeasts down to the species level, so a drug-resistant species can go unnoticed.
Everyone uses the toilet, whether they are ill or not, and whether or not they ever see a doctor. That makes wastewater a snapshot of a whole community.
During COVID, virus levels in sewage rose four to 14 days before confirmed cases did. For fungi, the evidence is still thin, and almost all of it concerns C. auris.

In southern Nevada in the US, researchers found it in 79% of wastewater samples over ten weeks, more often in areas served by healthcare facilities. In Florida, 47% of hospital wastewater samples tested positive, compared with 16% at treatment plants further downstream. In a UK hospital, the fungus was found in the wastewater coming from one particular ward during an outbreak.

These studies show that the fungus can be detected in wastewater. They do not yet show that sewage data can predict outbreaks. Nobody yet knows how much of the fungus each person sheds, so a sewage reading can’t be turned into a number of patients.

Genetic tests detect fungal DNA but can’t tell whether the fungus is alive or drug-resistant. Because many Candida species live harmlessly in people, simply finding one tells us little. Combining genetic tests with growing samples in the lab will be needed. And some fungi, such as Aspergillus, are inhaled and won’t pass through the gut, so sewage may not reflect those infections at all. Recent research picked up several disease-causing yeasts from wastewater sources, suggesting the approach could work beyond C. auris.

Wastewater treatment doesn’t remove every pathogen, while storm overflow pipes can release untreated sewage directly into rivers and the sea. C. auris has been found on remote beaches in the Andaman Islands, India, which suggests it lived in the environment long before it reached hospitals. In Hong Kong’s mangroves, all the multidrug-resistant yeasts researchers found came from sites near wastewater treatment works.
Low levels of antifungal drugs reaching rivers and soil may favour resistant strains. This link is possible but not yet proven.

Wastewater monitoring would not replace hospital testing of patients. Its value would be in telling health services where to look, especially in places where testing people at scale isn’t possible. Researchers now need to standardise methods, measure how much fungus people shed, and work out what sewage levels should trigger action. The goal should be to link wastewater data with hospital, animal and farm monitoring.
The tools already exist, as COVID showed. What has been missing is the will to prioritise fungi before the next resistant one outpaces us.
Pooja Padmakumar receives funding from Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) Digital Health Hub for AMR, project reference EP/X031276/1.

articles.title: The stroke risk younger adults may be overlooking – and the symptoms that should never be dismissed
articles.author: David Olawade, Lecturer, Department of Allied and Public Health, School of Health, Sport and Bioscience, University of East London
paras: Stroke is often seen as a condition that only affects older people. Yet the incidence of stroke in older people has actually fallen in recent decades. At the same time, rates of stroke in under-55s has been on the rise.

In England, stroke incidence among 35- to 54-year-olds rose by about 2% a year between 2001 and 2010, even as overall rates dropped. In Oxfordshire alone, stroke rates in under-55s were about 90% higher in 2010–2018 than in 1981–1986 – while rates in older people fell.
The US tells a similar story, with stroke rates in 20- to 54-year-olds rising from 34 to 62 cases per 100,000 people a year between 1993-1994 and 2020.

Globally, nearly 2.8 million people under 55 had a stroke in 2021, almost 90% of them in low- and middle-income countries. Between 2020 and 2030, it’s projected that rates of ischaemic stroke (the most common type, which is caused by a blood clot) among 20- to 39-year-olds will rise by about 12%.
What is fuelling the rise?
The rising rates of stroke in young people largely appears to be driven by things we can change.

A large international study identified ten modifiable risk factors which accounted for around 92% of strokes that occurred in people under 55. These factors included high blood pressure, physical inactivity, high cholesterol, poor diet, obesity, smoking, heart problems, diabetes, alcohol consumption and psychosocial factors (such as stress or poor mental health).
High blood pressure alone accounted for almost half of the strokes that occurred in people aged 55 and under. Lack of regular exercise accounted for more than a third.

A UK study, which looked at 1,765 people aged 18-49 who were hospitalised for a stroke, found 42% of patients had high blood pressure, 24% high cholesterol, 23% smoked and 14% had diabetes. About 7% reported recreational drug use.
Rates of obesity and diabetes have been rising in younger people for three decades. These conditions, along with high blood pressure, are often undiagnosed or undertreated in younger adults.

But left untreated, these health problems can quietly raise stroke risk. For instance, research found that under-55s with diabetes were about 3.5 times as likely to suffer a stroke or mini-stroke than those who didn’t have the condition. Those with high blood pressure were about 2.5 times as likely.

But these factors don’t explain everything. Around half of strokes in young people that were caused by a blood clot had no clear cause. Research also shows a growing number of the strokes experienced by young people have no known risk factor.

Researchers are now investigating alternative risk factors, including air pollution, autoimmune conditions and illicit drug use. Stress and overworking are also increasingly being linked to higher risk of stroke in young people.

Lack of awareness is part of the problem, too, as my systematic review showed. People who don’t see themselves as at risk are less likely to visit their doctor or change their lifestyle. Alongside risk factors that already go undetected, this may partly explain why stroke rates in younger adults haven’t fallen as they have in older people.
The signs young people miss
Stroke in younger adults can be easier to miss as well.

A large US analysis found that people aged 18-44 were the age group most likely to be sent home from emergency departments with a missed stroke, often after complaining of dizziness or headache. A Stroke Association survey also found a quarter of stroke survivors aged 60 and under said they were initially misdiagnosed.

The signs of a stroke in younger people can sometimes be different than they are in older people. While most people will look out for symptoms such as face drooping on one side, arms that can’t both be lifted and speech that’s slurred or confused, young people don’t always fit this pattern.

Strokes at the back of the brain, which affects balance and vision rather than the face and arms, are more common in young adults. In these cases, symptoms can manifest as problems with balance or eyesight, a headache, neck pain or vertigo.

Not only can these symptoms be missed by healthcare workers, young people themselves may explain them away as a migraine, tiredness, a hangover or an inner ear problem. Symptoms can also stop after a short time. Even if they do, you should still get medical help immediately.
Speed matters. Clot-busting treatment generally has to be given within 4.5 hours of symptoms starting. The sooner it’s given, the better the outcome and recovery.
The good news is that most strokes in younger people are linked to things we can change.

The first thing you can do to lower your risk is to know your blood pressure. High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so it’s important to have yours checked. You should also get checked for diabetes and high cholesterol, especially if you’re overweight or have a family history of heart disease or stroke.

Lifestyle matters, too. Don’t smoke, avoid recreational drugs and keep alcohol to no more than 14 units a week. It’s also recommended you eat less salt (no more than 6g a day) and more fibre, as these will help keep your blood pressure and cholesterol down.
Exercise is also key. Aim to get at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as fast walking or cycling.

You should also take stress and long working hours seriously. Both have been linked to a higher risk of stroke in their own right, even after accounting for other risk factors such as high blood pressure and smoking.
Stroke is no longer just an older person’s problem. Knowing the signs, and acting fast, could save your life or someone else’s.

David Olawade is a co-investigator on the Women’s Inclusion in Stroke Education and Readiness for Artificial Intelligence/Digital Technologies (WISER-AID) project, which is funded by the Burdett Trust for Nursing.

articles.title: I’m an athletic trainer – here’s how to know when kids sports are too intense
articles.author: Adam Annaccone, Clinical Associate Professor of Kinesiology, University of Texas at Arlington
paras: At a recent T-ball game, I was talking with another father who mentioned that his son had never played before. As we watched our children falling over trying to scoop up a ground ball, we laughed about how they were still figuring everything out. There was something refreshing about seeing kids learn a game without worrying about how well they were playing.

That moment stayed with me. I’ve spent years as an athletic trainer in collegiate and professional sports, helping athletes stay healthy, handle the demands of competition and perform at their best. Today, I’m a clinical associate professor of kinesiology and chief health and performance adviser for an NCAA Division I athletics program. Given my work, you might expect me to take an active role in developing my own children’s athletic abilities, especially in a youth sports culture where early specialization and greater commitment are often seen as advantages.

And I understand the appeal. Like any parent, I want my children to have opportunities, and it’s easy to wonder whether another practice or lesson might help them get ahead. But with twins who are nearly 6, I’m more interested in whether they enjoy sports than how good they become at them.

As they get older, particularly if they want to pursue sports seriously, my role as a parent will change. Right now, I can step back and let them explore. But as training and competition become more demanding, I’ll want to become more involved in understanding and questioning those demands. Research on training, recovery and athletic development can help parents navigate what’s appropriate as their children’s sports experiences intensify.

When I’m watching my children play, I’d rather be their dad than their performance coach. When they ask to practice hitting or throwing, I’m happy to help. They usually decide when we’re done. Twenty minutes? Great. Five minutes? That’s fine too.
Practice matters, but giving children some control over when and how they practice can help keep it from becoming another obligation.

Research involving more than 9,000 young athletes found that children tend to be more motivated to participate in sports when parents support their ability to make decisions about their participation.

As children get older, their goals may change. Some will want to compete at higher levels or focus on a particular sport. Those ambitions deserve support, but giving children a voice doesn’t mean parents should step away from important decisions. As commitments grow, parents may need to ask more questions about training schedules, recovery time and the expectations placed on their children.

I’ve heard parents describe traveling hours for youth sports tournaments, only to discover that many of the teams competing came from the same communities they had traveled from. One parent recalled driving to Houston for a tournament where six of the eight teams were from the Dallas-Fort Worth area.

I understand how families end up in these situations. An extra practice, private lessons or joining a more competitive team can each seem reasonable. Over time, those commitments become expectations, and saying no isn’t always easy when your child is part of a team.

But more training doesn’t automatically produce better athletes. My experience in sports medicine and performance has taught me that improvement depends on how athletes respond to training, not simply how much they do. Training places demands on the body, and athletes need time to adapt.

The American Academy of Pediatrics cautions that excessive training and early specialization are associated with increased overuse injury risk and may contribute to burnout. Risk depends on training volume, recovery and individual development, particularly during adolescence.

As training demands increase, parents should pay attention to how their children are responding, not just whether they’re experiencing pain. Persistent fatigue, declining performance, changes in sleep or a loss of enthusiasm may suggest that recovery isn’t keeping pace with training. Even an athlete who loves their sport can reach a point where the demands become too much. These are reasons for a parent to discuss the workload with their child and coaches, while persistent or worsening pain warrants medical evaluation.

Athletic development also benefits from variety. Running, climbing, jumping and exploring different activities can help develop coordination and a range of movement skills. The International Olympic Committee recommends varied physical activity and developmentally appropriate training, including for children who may eventually specialize.

Just as important is whether young athletes want to keep playing. Children who enjoy sports are more likely to want to continue participating, research shows. When young soccer players were asked what made sports fun, they identified working hard, improving and spending time with teammates. Even the best training program won’t accomplish much if an athlete no longer wants to participate.
Leaving the game at the field

In collegiate and professional sports, reviewing performance is routine. After competition, staff identify what worked, what didn’t and what needs attention. But children don’t need a performance review every time they climb into the car.

I let my children start conversations about their games. If they want to talk about a missed ball, something funny or something that upset them, I’ll listen. If they want to talk about something else, that’s fine too.

Researchers who recorded parent-child car rides around sporting events found that much of the time passed in silence and sports came up relatively infrequently. They also observed occasions when parents interrupted or provided feedback before children could respond. The findings don’t establish one right way to handle the drive home, but they offer parents a reason to consider whether their children want feedback in the first place.

No parent knows whether their child will become a competitive athlete, play recreationally or eventually find interests outside organized sports. I’m comfortable leaving that future open for my children. As a father, I’m far more interested in whether my kids will want to play again next week than how well they played today.

articles.title: What the measles vaccine’s ‘97% effective’ rating means for Pittsburgh parents
articles.author: Rebecca Smullin Dawson, Associate Professor of Biology, Allegheny College
paras: Pennsylvania is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades, with more than 1,400 confirmed cases and six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, according to statistics compiled by the state.

Each new case brings a new warning of a measles exposure in that community. Exposures have occurred at hospitals and doctors’ offices, grocery stores and restaurants, and K-12 schools and universities.

Exposure alerts come with the same instructions: Check your MMR vaccine status, and watch for symptoms for the next three weeks. People are told that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles. The underlying message is that if you’re vaccinated, you’re protected.
The MMR vaccine is highly effective at preventing disease, but it isn’t a guarantee. People may hear that 97% figure and wonder about the other 3%.

Parents ask me: Should I be worried? How do I know if my kid has measles? Do I need an MMR booster? Most recently, my teenage daughter texted me to ask about her MMR vaccine status. She was worried about what would happen if she were exposed.

These are questions I can answer as both a mother and an epidemiologist in northwestern Pennsylvania. I became both at once. My daughter was born at the start of my doctoral program, and I read epidemiology textbooks aloud to her while studying for my comprehensive exams. I defended my dissertation on my son’s due date. I’m a better mother because I’m an epidemiologist, and a better epidemiologist because I’m a mom.
Are these measles exposure alerts cause for alarm?
The advice in each public measles exposure alert matches the guidance doctors follow when a patient may have been exposed.

Everyone is asked to watch for symptoms, whether or not they’re vaccinated. The number of unvaccinated people across Pennsylvania is growing. As a result, many communities, including Allegheny County, no longer have herd immunity.
Four of the over 1,400 confirmed measles cases in Pennsylvania were people who had been vaccinated. These cases are known as breakthrough infections.

The term “herd immunity” wasn’t coined until 1918. That year, a veterinarian wrote about an outbreak of “contagious abortion” in sheep and cattle, a literal herd. Today, herd immunity means that the risk of disease for susceptible people, those without immunity, drops when they are surrounded by people who are immune.

In other words, if the people around you are immune, you’re unlikely to get sick even if you’re susceptible. For measles, that protection depends on about 95% of people being immune. In a school or community where fewer than 95% of people are vaccinated, measles can spread more easily.
In Allegheny County, 93.8% of children are fully vaccinated against measles. Some neighborhoods are above 97% uptake, while others are below the necessary 95% needed for herd immunity.
What happens after an exposure?

Measles exposures are announced publicly by the Department of Health and local healthcare providers. During a measles outbreak, public health departments may get in touch with close contacts to alert them to an exposure.

Public exposure alerts, like the one made in October after there was a measles exposure at a Target near Pittsburgh, are also used. Public alerts are for settings where exposed people can’t be identified and contacted individually. Measles is so contagious that a single case can infect up to 18 susceptible people.
Measles spreads through the air and through respiratory droplets, like those released when someone sneezes. The virus can also survive outside the body, lingering in the air and on surfaces.

Imagine I have measles and walk into my local grocery store. I’m contagious from about four days before the rash appears until four days after. Every time I breathe out, I release virus particles into the air, and those particles can stay infectious for up to two hours. If I sneeze in the produce section, the virus can survive on surfaces for up to two hours.

However, if you’ve had measles or were vaccinated with two doses of the MMR vaccine, you are protected. Two doses provides 97% lifetime protection against measles. This means that even without herd immunity, fewer than 3% of individuals with immunity are likely to contract measles. Adults who have had measles, or who have documentation of the recommended doses of the MMR vaccine, don’t need a booster.

People who were vaccinated between 1963 and 1967, or who aren’t sure which vaccine they received, should talk to their primary care provider about whether they need another dose. This is because the measles vaccine used between those years was not as effective as the MMR vaccine that is currently given.

Today, children typically get their first dose of the MMR vaccine at 12 to 15 months old and a second dose at 4 to 6 years old. Because the vaccine is given in early childhood, people born in the early to mid-1960s are the most likely to have received the older vaccine. People born before 1957 are generally considered immune, because measles was so widespread then that almost everyone caught it as a child.
What are the symptoms of measles?

Symptoms of measles include a high fever that can reach 105 degrees Fahrenheit (40.6 degrees Celsius), a cough, a runny nose and conjunctivitis, also known as pin keye. These symptoms overlap with those of other respiratory viruses, such as flu and COVID-19.

Most people with measles develop a red, blotchy rash. It starts on the face and spreads down the body, like paint poured from a bucket. People who are immunocompromised or were previously vaccinated, even with one dose of the MMR vaccine, may not develop the rash. Between 25% and 40% of immunocompromised people with measles never get the rash.
A telltale sign of measles is Koplik spots, tiny white spots inside the mouth that can show up a day or two before the rash.
Why does measles keep making headlines?

Measles can have serious consequences. About 1 in 20 people with measles develop pneumonia, and up to 3 in 1,000 cases end in death. Children younger than 5 and adults older than 20 are most likely to experience these severe complications.

Without herd immunity in many communities, measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths in Pennsylvania are likely to keep rising. The state Department of Health reports community spread of measles in 14 of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties.

Each of these cases is mostly preventable with the MMR vaccine. The U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000, meaning it was no longer spreading continuously here. This year’s outbreak shows how quickly that can change and the negative health consequences it can have in our communities.

articles.title: Is natural toothpaste really as good as fluoride? Tooth decay expert on the difference
articles.author: Aylin Baysan, Professor of Cariology in relation to Minimally Invasive Dentistry, Queen Mary University of London
paras: Natural, herbal and organic toothpastes are becoming familiar sights on shop shelves, often promoted as healthier alternatives to conventional products. Some contain ingredients such as aloe vera, neem or green tea. But before changing toothpaste, there is one important question to consider: does it contain fluoride?

Fluoride is a mineral that helps protect teeth against decay. Some toothpastes marketed as natural contain it, while others do not. The words on the front of the tube cannot tell us whether a product will protect our teeth.

These terms are often used interchangeably, although they mean different things. “Natural” usually describes ingredients derived from natural sources. “Herbal” refers to plant-based ingredients, while “organic” generally describes ingredients produced to particular farming standards. None of these labels, on its own, shows that a toothpaste can prevent tooth decay.

The range of products is considerable. A 2021 UK study examined 500 toothpastes, from 95 brands with alternative formats such as tooth powders and solid toothpaste tablets. Nearly a third contained no fluoride, and some did not clearly state their fluoride content. The study examined products available to buy, so it cannot tell us how many people actually use fluoride-free toothpaste.
Why fluoride makes a difference

Tooth decay begins when bacteria in dental plaque, a sticky film that builds up on teeth, feed on sugars from food and drinks. They produce acids that damage enamel, the hard outer surface of the tooth. Over time, this can lead to holes, or cavities.

Fluoride helps enamel resist acid and repair early damage before a cavity forms. Its benefits are supported by decades of research. A 2019 Cochrane review, which brought together results from 96 studies, found that brushing with fluoride toothpaste reduced tooth decay compared with brushing with toothpaste without fluoride. Reviews bring together findings from multiple studies to assess the overall evidence.
Yet people sometimes switch to fluoride-free products because they believe natural ingredients must be safer or healthier.

In a 2019 letter to the British Dental Journal, my colleague and I described a dental student who had developed several cavities after changing to a fluoride-free organic toothpaste. The student had other risk factors, including a history of sugary snacking and infrequent dental visits. We can not say that this single case cannot show that the organic toothpaste caused multiple decays, but this clearly illustrates why checking for fluoride is important, even for people who brush their teeth regularly.
The evidence for herbal toothpaste

Some toothpastes and mouthwashes contain plant extracts, including green tea, aloe vera and neem, a tree traditionally used for oral hygiene in South Asia. These ingredients may help control bacteria and gum inflammation – also called gingivitis – which can cause redness, swelling and bleeding when brushing.

A 2024 review of earlier research suggested that some herbal oral-care products, particularly mouthwashes, could reduce plaque and gum inflammation as effectively as conventional products. But many of the studies were short, and their methods with the results varied. This makes it difficult to know how well particular ingredients work over time.

Reducing plaque and gum inflammation is useful, but it does not prove that a toothpaste prevents cavities. There is insufficient evidence that herbal ingredients can replace fluoride’s established protection against tooth decay. A toothpaste can contain plant ingredients and fluoride, so consumers do not necessarily have to choose between them.

Charcoal toothpaste is another product often marketed as natural, particularly for whitening teeth. A 2023 review found limited evidence that charcoal toothpastes whitened teeth better than other options. Most studies also suggested that they could be more abrasive: they might wear away the tooth surface through rubbing. However, most of the research was conducted in laboratories, so it cannot establish how much wear occurs with everyday use.
How to choose a toothpaste

The simplest way to choose a toothpaste is to check the fluoride concentration on its packaging. In the UK, NHS advice is that adults should use toothpaste containing at least 1,350 parts per million (ppm) fluoride. This means at least 1,350 parts of fluoride for every million parts of toothpaste.

Children need the right strength and amount for their age. The NHS recommends at least 1,000ppm for children under three, using just a smear. Children aged three to six should use a pea-sized amount of toothpaste containing 1,000–1,500ppm fluoride. From age seven, the recommended concentration is 1,350–1,500ppm.

Tooth-brushing twice a day for about two minutes, including last thing at night, and spit out the excess toothpaste rather than rinsing immediately with water would be beneficial. This leaves fluoride on the teeth for longer. A dentist can advise if someone needs extra protection against tooth decay.

Lastly, natural ingredients may have a useful place in oral care, and better long-term studies could establish more about their benefits. But labels such as “natural” or “organic” are no substitute for evidence. Whatever else a toothpaste contains, an appropriate amount of fluoride currently remains one of the simplest and cost-effective ways to protect teeth.

articles.title: This weightlifting technique can help older adults stay fit and independent as they age
articles.author: Liam T. Pearson-Noseworthy, Distinguished Teaching Fellow, School of Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation, Northumbria University, Newcastle
paras: If you’re over 60 and have started lifting weights, you’ve probably been told to take it slowly. Lift steadily, lower steadily, keep it controlled.

This may sound like sensible advice, but lifting slowly isn’t always better. While the technique may have an edge when it comes to building strength and muscle, lifting with speed may be the better option if you want to stay fit and keep moving well for years to come.

Most people associate weightlifting with building muscle and strength. But lifting can also build power (how quickly our muscles can produce force). This aspect of fitness fades earlier and faster than strength does as we age.

Part of the reason for this sits inside the muscle itself. Our muscles are made up of two types of fibres: slow-twitch fibres, which are built for endurance, and fast-twitch fibres, which are built for speed and help produce force quickly. While our slow-twitch fibres tend to hold up fairly well with age, our fast-twitch fibres tend to shrink and weaken.

The weakening of these fast-twitch fibres can have a significant impact on daily life as we get older. Even things as simple as climbing stairs or crossing the road before the lights change all benefit from power.

Muscle power may even matter more than strength when it comes to staying mobile. A study of 839 older adults in Italy compared how much power people could produce pushing with one leg with how hard they could push against a fixed resistance. The researchers found those with low leg power were two to three times more likely to have limited mobility than those with low strength.

Power matters for trips and falls too. When you catch your toe, your standing leg has to push off quickly and forcefully, which gives your other foot time to swing forward and land in the right place. Being less able to generate muscle force as you age may mean it’s harder to stop yourself from falling if you trip.

A study of 94 older adults compared people who’d had a fall in the past year with those who hadn’t. Both groups had similar strength in their knees, but those who’d fallen had less leg power, estimated from how quickly they could stand up from a chair five times.
Because the study looked back at falls, it can’t tell us whether low power caused the fall or if recovering from the fall caused the loss of power. But it fits with the trip research.

The good news is that training can help. In a very small pilot study of just nine people, 16 weeks of leg strength training increased how hard they could push off with their legs. Those who trained also tended to respond better after a trip than those who didn’t, though the difference was too small to be certain.
But in order to build muscle power, you need to lift a little differently than you would to build strength.
Training strength usually means lifting and lowering the weight at a controlled, comfortable pace. To train power, you still lower the weight under control, but try to lift it quickly and with force.

A large review of 20 trials and 566 older adults compared lifting fast with lifting more slowly. Lifting fast gave a bigger boost to muscle power and also provided modest benefits to everyday physical function.
When it comes to strength, the picture is more mixed. In that same review, strength and muscle gains were the same either way.
My 2022 review of 12 trials conducted in people over 60 found strength gains leaned towards faster lifting – though this finding wasn’t very robust, as the studies were small and often low quality.

I also conducted a trial in 31 untrained adults aged 60 to 79 where they did one leg press session a week for six weeks. Whether they pushed fast or slow, their strength, everyday function and quality of life all improved. However, the slow groups tended to gain a little more strength, while the fast groups tended to improve more on everyday tasks.

A 2026 review of 16 studies in adults aged 60 and over found that slower lifting tended to come out ahead for muscle size and strength, while faster lifting tended to come out ahead on tests of everyday physical function.
So technique may matter depending on your goals. Slower lifting may build somewhat more strength and muscle, while faster lifting may help more with everyday tasks.

But it’s important to note that fast lifting isn’t a cure-all. That same review of 20 trials found this technique made no clear difference when it came to improving balance. For preventing falls and improving balance, the strongest evidence is for balance and functional exercise – movements that copy daily life, such as stepping and turning. Combining these exercises with strength training may cut the number of falls by about a third.
Building power doesn’t mean you have to change your entire weightlifting routine. All it takes is one small simple technique change.

When lifting, lower the weight slowly and under control. Then, push it back up as fast as you can while keeping good form. Pick a light-to-moderate weight, something you could lift perhaps 15 times with good form, then stop well short of that, at around eight reps, so every rep still moves quickly.

The same is true if you’re performing bodyweight exercises at home. If you’re doing a chair squat, for example, aim to sit slowly before standing up as quickly as you safely can. Use your hands on the armrests if you need to.
The weight itself doesn’t have to move fast. What matters is that you’re trying to move it as quickly as you safely can.
Weightlifting has many benefits for our health as we age. Just make sure to train power as well as strength to help you stay mobile for longer.
